patients.label: 75-year-old man with right upper quadrant pain and a subhepatic abscess after appendectomy for perforated appendicitis
attribution_limitations: The abstract places the abscess five months after the appendectomy, while the case text gives the appendectomy as six months prior to presentation with a five-month history of pain.
The abscess is called a hepatic abscess, a right subhepatic abscess and a localized abscess adjacent to the liver capsule in different places.
The appendicolith is said to have likely escaped the lumen during perforation or to have been dropped during surgery; the mechanism is not established.
The discussion says the abscess was originally misdiagnosed, while the case text says the lesion was initially interpreted as a possible simple liver cyst.

evidence.quote: Right upper quadrant ultrasound demonstrating a cystic lesion at the inferior aspect of the right hepatic lobe (subcapsular region). The lesion appears anechoic with well-defined borders and no solid components, initially interpreted as a simple hepatic cyst.

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the abdomen showing a rim-enhancing fluid collection posterior to the right hepatic lobe. The peripheral enhancement and adjacent hepatic capsule involvement are consistent with a localized subhepatic abscess.

CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis performed six months earlier during the patient’s presentation with acute perforated appendicitis, demonstrating two calcified appendicoliths in the right lower quadrant, near the inflamed and perforated appendix.

Post-operative CT scan obtained several weeks after appendectomy revealing a small round radiodensity along the posterior surface of the liver within the subhepatic space, retrospectively consistent with a retained appendicolith that later served as the nidus for abscess formation.

claims.text: A 75-year-old man with hypertension, who had undergone an open appendectomy for perforated acute appendicitis six months prior, presented to his primary care physician with a five-month history of persistent, dull, intermittent right upper quadrant pain. He denied fever, chills and jaundice. He had mild RUQ tenderness without peritoneal signs, moderately elevated C-reactive protein and sedimentation rate, a mildly elevated white blood cell count of 11×10^(9)/L, and normal liver enzymes.
